'''Brian John O'Brien''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AO|FTSE}} (27 February 1934 – 7 August 2020) was an Australian physicist and space scientist. He is best known for his "research into lunar dust and the challenges it presents for exploration of the Moon." He "highlighted how hazardous it was for astronauts and their equipment."<ref name="uwa-legacy">{{cite web |title=UWA physicist leaves behind stellar legacy |url=https://www.uwa.edu.au/news/Article/2020/August/UWA-physicist-leaves-behind-stellar-legacy |website=www.uwa.edu.au |publisher=University of Western Australia |access-date=23 December 2020 |language=en-AU |date=13 August 2020}}</ref> Five experiments designed by him were placed on the Moon by the [[Apollo 11]] Mission. One measured radiation, the others were concerned with [[Moon dust]].<ref name="atse-dream" />

O'Brien also designed the [[Charged Particle Lunar Environment Experiment]] (CPLEE), placed on the lunar surface by the [[Apollo 14]] mission as part of the [[Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package]] (ALSEP).<ref name="nasa-cplee">{{cite web |title=Charged Particle Lunar Environment Experiment (CPLEE) |url=https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/experiment/display.action?id=1971-008C-08 |website=nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov |publisher=NASA |date=14 May 2020 |access-date=23 December 2020}}</ref>

After studying physics at [[Sydney University]], O'Brien worked as a physicist in Antarctica. There he saw the [[aurora australis]], which led to his space career.<ref name="9news-moon-mission"/>

He was a NASA principal investigator. For his radiation experiment, he was awarded the [[NASA Medal for Exceptional Scientific Achievement]]. He was the first Australian so awarded.<ref name="atse-dream" />

O'Brien was a professor of space science at [[Rice University]], Houston, from 1963 to 1968, and adjunct professor of physics at the [[University of Western Australia]] from 2009 until 2020.<ref name="atse-dream" />

He later moved to Perth with his wife,  Avril, and headed the [[Environmental Protection Authority of Western Australia]].<ref name="9news-moon-mission">{{cite news |last1=Sara |first1=Swain |title=Exclusive: Aussie scientist's special moon landings mission |url=https://www.nine.com.au/australia-news/moon-landings-anniversary-50-nasa-australian-scientist-brian-obrien-perth-20190706-p5x66v.html |access-date=23 December 2020 |work=9News |publisher=Nine Digital Pty Ltd |date=6 July 2019}}</ref>

O'Brien was elected a Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Technological Sciences and Engineering]] (FTSE)<ref name="atse-dream"/> in 1993.

He died on 7 August 2020, aged 86.<ref name="atse-dream">{{cite web |last1=O'Brien |first1=Brian |title="Dream with me, please" – remembering Brian O'Brien, who reached for the moon |url=https://www.atse.org.au/news-and-events/article/dream-with-me-please-remembering-brian-obrien-who-reached-for-the-moon/ |publisher=Australian Academy of Technology and Engineering |website=atse.org.au  |date=July 2009 |access-date=23 December 2020 |language=en-AU}} Originally published in ''The Sydney Morning Herald''</ref>

O'Brien was posthumously made an [[Officer of the Order of Australia]] (AO) in the [[2021 Australia Day Honours]].<ref name=pmc-oz-day-2021-ao>{{cite web |title=The late Dr Brian John O'BRIEN - Officer of the Order of Australia |url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/2008262 |website=honours.pmc.gov.au |publisher=Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet |access-date=29 January 2021 |date=25 January 2021}}</ref>
